scenes.title: templatefile and Cloud-Init
scenes.narration: A Linux machine that installs nginx on first boot — configured not in Terraform code, and not by hand, but from a template. This lesson introduces templatefile: render a file with variables, hand it to the VM, and let cloud-init do the rest.

scenes.heading: What you'll learn
points: templatefile(PATH, VARS): render a file with substituted values
cloud-init: the first-boot bootstrap script for Linux VMs
custom_data on azurerm_linux_virtual_machine — must be base64-encoded
SSH key auth instead of passwords for the Linux VM
scenes.narration: Here's what you'll learn. One: templatefile — render a file with substituted values. Two: cloud-init — the first-boot bootstrap script for Linux V Ms. Three: custom data on azurerm linux virtual machine — which must be base sixty-four encoded. Four: S S H key authentication instead of passwords for the Linux V M.

scenes.heading: Where this lab fits
points: Lab 24 of the Foundations section
Labs 17 and 21 built Windows VMs — passwords and data disks
Linux VMs bootstrap differently: cloud-init, not a script you paste
scenes.narration: This is lab twenty-four, and it switches the operating system. Windows machines — like the ones in earlier labs — are configured after login. Linux machines can bootstrap themselves on first boot, and today we write that bootstrap as a template file instead of burying a script inside the configuration.

scenes.heading: Templates keep scripts out of the configuration
points: cloud-init.tpl is a plain file with ${ } and %{ for %} directives
templatefile(PATH, VARS) substitutes them at plan time
custom_data must be base64-encoded — the VM decodes it on boot
Change the template → Terraform updates custom_data → VM re-runs it
scenes.narration: The mental model: the template is a separate file, and the configuration stays about infrastructure. Templatefile takes the path and a map of values, and produces the finished text. The template speaks two languages: dollar-brace for single values, and percent-brace blocks for loops. Keep big scripts out of dot t f files — cleaner to read, easier to reuse.

scenes.narration: The lab is in the course GitHub repository under Section 1, Foundations, link in the description. Note the new file: cloud-init dot t p l — the template that gets rendered.

The template itself — and it's not Terraform. Cloud-config format, read by cloud-init on first boot. Hostname comes from a variable, package update, and a loop over the packages list — nginx and curl. Then two commands: enable nginx, and write a homepage that proves the bootstrap ran.

Where the template becomes real. Templatefile takes the path and a map — hostname web dash templatefile, packages nginx and curl — and returns the finished text. It runs at plan time: the rendered result is part of the configuration from that moment on, stored inside the local named rendered.

The Linux machine. Custom data must be base64-encoded — so the rendered text goes through base64encode before the VM receives it. Authentication is an S S H key from a sensitive variable — no password anywhere. On first boot, cloud-init decodes the data and runs it: nginx installs itself.

scenes.caption: From template to first boot
scenes.narration: The pipeline, drawn out: the template file and the values map feed templatefile, which produces the finished script. Base64-encode it, and it lands in the machine's custom data — executed by cloud-init, once, on first boot. The configuration never contains the script; it contains the recipe for producing it.

steps.narration: Two inputs: the cloud-init template, and the values map.
templatefile substitutes both — hostname in place, packages looped.
The result is base64-encoded and set as custom data on the machine.
Cloud-init runs it once, on first boot — nginx installs itself.

scenes.narration: Apply time — five resources, and the machine takes about two minutes. The output command then prints the preview: the rendered template, with the hostname substituted and the package loop expanded. That preview is how you check the substitution without decoding base64 by hand.

scenes.heading: Common pitfall — raw template markers in comments
points: %{ and ${ } inside a comment are still parsed as directives
A stray ${ in the template breaks rendering at plan time
custom_data only runs cloud-init on FIRST boot — changes need care
Use %{ ~ to trim whitespace when a loop must not leave blank lines
scenes.narration: Here are the pitfalls in this lab. One: percent brace and dollar brace inside a comment are still parsed as directives. In a Terraform file, hash means comment; in a template, hash is just text — and any directive inside it stays live. Two: a stray dollar brace in the template breaks rendering at plan time. Any accidental interpolation fails the whole template — that's why the lab's template spells its markers out in words. Three: custom data runs cloud-init on first boot only — changes need care. Editing the template later doesn't re-run the script on an existing machine. Four: use the percent brace tilde form to trim whitespace, so a loop doesn't leave blank lines. Keep template files free of stray interpolation, even in comments.

points: templatefile(PATH, VARS): substitute ${ } values and %{ for %} loops
cloud-init.tpl stays a separate file — configuration stays clean
custom_data must be base64encode(...) — the VM decodes on first boot
SSH key auth via admin_ssh_key — no passwords on Linux VMs
terraform output rendered_preview shows the substitution worked
scenes.narration: Quick recap — five things. One: templatefile takes a path and a vars map — substituting dollar brace values and percent brace loops. Two: the cloud-init t p l stays a separate file — configuration stays clean. Three: custom data must be base sixty four encoded — the v m decodes it on first boot. Four: s s h key auth via the admin s s h key resource — no passwords on linux v m s. Five: the rendered preview output shows the substitution worked.
Now that we understand how this Terraform configuration works, in the next part of this video, we'll move to a real-world demo and deploy it in Microsoft Azure.
